title.en: Prefer slices and marginals over solid distributions

summary: Encode multivariate distributions with sections, marginals and conditionals rather than relying on perceived volume or opacity.
objective: Choose an encoding for a distribution that a viewer can actually read quantitatively.
applies_when: A joint distribution over two or more variables is displayed.
A three-dimensional density, cloud or volume rendering is being considered.
The viewer must compare regions or read a conditional relationship.
example_prompts: Show the joint density and let me take conditional slices.
Compare the spread of these two variables.
negative_signals: Single-variable distributions, where the area encoding already works.
Cases where the spatial structure itself is the subject rather than the probability.
not_for: Single-variable distributions, where the area encoding already works.
Cases where the spatial structure itself is the subject rather than the probability.

principles: Perceived volume and accumulated transparency are risky quantitative channels: occlusion hides the far side, and the apparent intensity of a volume rendering depends on the viewing direction and the transfer function rather than on the density alone. This record treats that as a design risk to test with your audience, not as a measured perceptual result.
Slices, marginals and conditionals reduce the problem to encodings that are readable, and they correspond to the questions people actually ask about a joint distribution.
A three-dimensional presentation earns its cost only when the third axis carries structure that projections destroy, such as a genuinely trivariate interaction.
Whatever the encoding, the quantity being encoded must be stated: density, cumulative probability, count or estimate are different things.
implementation: Offer a marginal for each variable and a conditional slice control, driven from the same underlying distribution as any spatial view.
If a volume view is used, pair it with a section plane the viewer can move, and label whether opacity encodes density or accumulated probability.
State the estimator when the distribution comes from data, including bandwidth or binning, since those change the picture.
Keep the axes and their units visible, and use a legend that maps the visual channel to the quantity.
Where regions must be compared, provide a numeric readout for the selected regions instead of relying on perception.
observable_checks: Ask a comparison question, such as which region carries more probability, and confirm the display supports a numeric answer.
Rotate a volume view and check whether the apparent density changes with viewing angle, which reveals an accumulation artefact.
Confirm the marginal panels are computed from the same distribution as the spatial view.
Change the estimator parameters and observe how much of the visible structure survives.

creative_affordances: Expressive volume renderings remain valuable for conveying overall shape when quantitative reading is not claimed.
Small-multiple conditional slices are often more beautiful as well as more readable than one dense cloud.
known_limits: Authored presentation guidance; it cites no perceptual study and reports no user testing.
No runtime rendering has been evaluated for this record.
